description: Set, lighting, sound and costume choices that capture the squalor and beauty of Jo's flat.
content_html:
The Flat as a World

Almost the entire action of A Taste of Honey takes place in a single rented flat in Salford. This is not merely a practical limitation — it is a central dramatic statement. The flat is cramped, damp, poorly lit, and overlooked by industrial chimneys. For a set designer, this single location both constrains and liberates: every entrance and exit carries weight, every object accumulates meaning, and the quality of light changes with the seasons as the play moves from winter to summer and back.

The set design for this play invites a fundamental choice: how literally do you render the flat’s squalor? A fully naturalistic set — peeling wallpaper, a functional kitchen with a practical gas ring, second-hand furniture, a single window casting grey northern light — roots the audience in the kitchen-sink tradition from which the play emerged. Alternatively, a more selective, spare set signals the play’s Brechtian dimension: a few key pieces (a table, two chairs, a rail for coats) that the audience fills in with imagination.

Key Fact

The single-setting structure concentrates the audience’s attention on the quality of life inside the flat. Every set object — Helen’s fashion magazines, Jo’s drawings pinned to the wall, the gas ring used for cooking and for warming the room — can function as a prop as symbol, communicating character, class and aspiration without dialogue.

Lighting: Bare Bulb to Candlelight

The play’s lighting opportunities are rich, precisely because the flat has almost no natural glamour to illuminate. A practical bare overhead bulb as the flat’s primary light source creates an authentic austerity: functional, unflattering, honest. From this base state, a lighting designer can make deliberate departures that carry meaning. When Jo and the Boy have their winter scenes together, a slightly warmer gel — amber through a Fresnel from a low angle — can create the illusion of fire or candlelight, transforming the same cramped flat into a briefly tender space. This is not decorating the scene — it is the designer communicating the warmth these two characters create for each other inside a cold world.

Contrast is equally important. When Helen returns at the end of the play, a harder, cooler lighting state — a blue-white overhead wash, the shadows harder — can signal how her presence changes the emotional temperature of the flat. The transition between these states does not need to be slow or obvious; a subtle cross-fade of a few seconds, registered almost subconsciously by the audience, is often more powerful than a dramatic blackout.

Strong exam answers for A Taste of Honey name specific lantern types and their qualities. A Fresnel lantern produces a soft-edged beam — useful for warm domestic scenes, where hard shadows would feel wrong. A profile (or ellipsoidal) lantern produces a sharply defined beam, useful for a tight lighting special when Jo addresses the audience directly. A flood gives a broad, unfocused wash — right for lighting the flat’s general domestic interior. A gobo (pattern plate) inside a profile could project the industrial chimneys’ silhouette onto the back wall, fusing set and light to suggest the world outside without building it. All these choices communicate meaning; none is merely technical.

Sound: The World Beyond the Flat

Because the play is set almost entirely indoors, sound design carries the weight of evoking the larger world: Salford’s industrial soundscape, the canal, the fairground, the street. A sound cue of distant tram bells before Jo and the Boy’s first scene places the flat inside a specific, living city. The sound of a foghorn from the canal during the winter sequence hints at departures — the Boy will soon sail on — without any character needing to say so.

The jazz musicians are the most distinctive element of the play’s sound world. They occupy the stage visibly and their music bridges scene changes, underscores action and comments on the characters. A sound designer in a production without live musicians must make a deliberate choice: do they use recorded jazz from speakers (which loses the Brechtian visibility) or find another solution? Either choice carries a directorial statement about the play’s form. Live music foregrounds the theatrical artifice; recorded music from hidden speakers nudges the production towards naturalism.

Key Fact

Sound design in A Taste of Honey operates on two levels: the jazz musicians as a theatrical, Brechtian element commenting on the action; and the ambient soundscape of 1950s Salford — trams, factories, the canal — rooting the play in its specific time and place. Strong design answers name specific sounds, their source (live or recorded, directional speaker placement) and their effect on the audience’s understanding of a named moment.

Costume: Two Women, Two Worlds

Costume design in A Taste of Honey immediately communicates the class and aspirational differences between Jo and Helen. Helen’s fur coat — worn, slightly past its best, but glamorous in intent — tells the audience before any dialogue that she is a woman who performs a version of herself: worldly, unconcerned, not domesticated. The coat is armour and advertisement at once. Jo’s clothing, by contrast, is practical and worn: a school uniform in early scenes, then clothes that look functional rather than fashionable. The contrast between these two women, standing together in the flat, is itself a visual argument about what options 1950s society offered women of their class.

For a designer working in period, fabric choice matters: the difference between a wool coat and a nylon one, between a cotton school dress and a synthetic fibre, is visible and period-specific. Costume choice should also account for how the garment moves — Helen swirls, Jo hunches. Physical interpretation is inseparable from costume: how a character inhabits their clothes tells the audience as much as the clothes themselves.

A weak exam answer says “I would costume the characters in 1950s clothing to show the period.” A strong answer goes further: it specifies fabric, colour, fit, silhouette, and the meaning each choice creates. Helen’s fur coat in a muted camel colour signals aspiration without wealth; a brighter colour (red, yellow) would signal something different about her desire to be noticed. Peter’s slightly better-cut suit, compared to the Boy’s simpler clothes, communicates class difference at a glance. Geof’s paint-stained art-student clothing — practical, creative, slightly outside convention — tells the audience he belongs to a different social world from Peter’s. Each of these details requires a justified design choice, not just a period reference.
exam_tip_html:
For 8-mark designer questions, the most common error is giving one idea per discipline without justifying what it means. A strong answer picks a specific moment, names the design element (e.g. “a Fresnel lantern with an amber gel from a low side angle”) and explains the precise effect on the audience at that moment (“creating the warmth of candlelight and signalling the characters’ brief intimacy despite the flat’s cold exterior”). Avoid generic descriptors like “atmospheric lighting” or “period costume” — every choice must be justified with a named effect.

For 20-mark extended staging questions, you must cover set, lighting, sound, costume AND at least one performer choice. Anchor all choices to a named scene or moment in the play. Explain why each choice serves the play’s themes — the gap between aspiration and reality, the world that presses in on the flat, the play’s hybrid naturalistic/Brechtian form.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The single-setting structure makes every design choice in the flat carry double weight — stage objects function as props and symbols simultaneously, communicating character, class and aspiration without relying on dialogue.
  • Lighting in A Taste of Honey ranges from a bare functional bulb (austerity, honesty) to tender amber warmth (intimacy) to cooler, harder states (emotional chill) — strong answers name lantern type, gel colour and intensity, not just “mood.”
  • Costume design reveals character before dialogue: Helen’s fur coat performs worldliness and aspiration; Jo’s functional clothing communicates her limited options. Fabric, colour, silhouette and how the character inhabits the garment are all meaningful design decisions.

practice_questions.text: Name one type of lantern a lighting designer might use to create a soft, warm domestic atmosphere in A Taste of Honey.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of: Fresnel lantern / flood / PAR can. (Profile/ellipsoidal is also acceptable if the student explains it produces a focused effect rather than soft wash — credit the explanation.)

practice_questions.text: What is a gobo in lighting design?
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as a metal (or glass) plate inserted into a profile lantern; 1 mark for explaining that it projects a pattern or texture onto the stage/set.

practice_questions.text: Explain how a costume designer might use Helen's fur coat to communicate her character and social position in A Taste of Honey. Refer to specific costume choices.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: identification of the fur coat as a costume choice (1); explanation of its fabric/silhouette/condition (slightly worn, aspirational) and what this communicates about Helen's social position (1); link to character — Helen performs worldliness and independence (1); effect on the audience — they read her character before she speaks (1).

practice_questions.text: As a lighting designer, explain how you would design the lighting for a moment when Jo and the Boy share their brief winter intimacy inside the flat. Refer to specific lighting choices and their effect on the audience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Specific lighting state named with lantern type (e.g. Fresnel with amber gel from a low, warm angle); justification of why this quality of light evokes warmth and candlelight in the cold flat; contrast with the flat's base lighting state (bare overhead bulb, cooler wash) so the audience feels the shift; explanation of what this communicates about the characters' relationship; possible use of a gobo to suggest firelight flicker or shadows; effect on audience named (intimacy, fragility, the sense that this warmth is temporary). All choices anchored to the named moment.

Secure: Named lighting choice with some justification; at least one specific design element (gel, lantern, intensity); link to character relationship and audience effect; generally concrete.

Developing: General lighting described (warm, soft) without naming lantern or gel; effect on audience stated but not developed; little link to the moment's meaning.

Emerging: Basic description (bright or dim lights) with no design specifics; no link to meaning or audience effect.

practice_questions.text: Analyse what Delaney intends the audience to understand about class and aspiration through the design of the flat and its contrast with the world outside in A Taste of Honey.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis of how the flat's design communicates class — the gap between the domestic interior and the industrial Salford outside; how props-as-symbols (Helen's fashion magazines, Jo's drawings) reveal character aspiration against limited circumstance; how the sound of the world outside (trams, canal, chimneys) presses in on the flat; analysis of Delaney's intention to make the audience feel the weight of limited options on these women, not judge them; specific reference to design choices and their effect at named moments. Substantiated critical judgement.

Secure: Clear analysis of flat as a symbol of class; design choices referenced (set, sound or costume); link to Delaney's intentions; some engagement with audience effect.

Developing: Relevant points about the flat's squalor; some reference to design; limited analysis of intention; effect implied not stated.

Emerging: Descriptive account of the flat's appearance; little analysis of why Delaney constructs it this way.

practice_questions.text: As a director, discuss how you would use set design, lighting, sound and costume to bring the opening scene of A Taste of Honey to life for a contemporary audience. Your answer should communicate the play's social context and the relationship between Jo and Helen.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full directorial vision; staging configuration named and justified (e.g. end-on proscenium with sight of jazz musicians upstage); set design specific (peeling wallpaper, practical bare bulb, cramped furniture, industrial backdrop or projected chimney shadow using gobo); lighting state for the opening (cool, flat overhead wash establishing austerity; transition to warmer state when characters' dynamic shifts); sound design specific (tram bells off-stage left, jazz musicians launching into an up-tempo tune as Helen and Jo arrive, soundscape of the city pressing in); costume choices with named fabrics and silhouettes (Helen's worn camel fur coat vs Jo's school-coat with buttons missing); performer choices including vocal register (Salford accents, Helen's breezy pace vs Jo's sharper responses) and physical staging (Helen taking the centre stage, Jo circling the edges); all choices linked to class, aspiration and the play's social context. Substantiated and convincing.

Secure: Most design areas addressed with some concrete choices; staging configuration referenced; character relationship communicated through design; at least one specific design detail per discipline.

Developing: Two or three design areas mentioned; some specifics but patchily; performer choices thin; limited link to social context.

Emerging: Listing of basic staging ideas; few or no specific design elements; social context not engaged.

knowledge_checks.q: What kind of lantern produces a soft-edged beam suitable for warm domestic lighting?
In A Taste of Honey, what does Helen's fur coat communicate to the audience before she speaks?
options: She performs worldliness and aspiration despite limited means
She is mourning a recent loss
She is dressed for cold Salford weather only

knowledge_checks.q: A gobo is a metal plate inserted into a profile lantern that projects a _____ onto the stage.
A _____ is a stage object that carries symbolic meaning beyond its practical function.
Match each design discipline to its key decision in A Taste of Honey:
right: How literally to render the flat's squalor — naturalistic or selective
Bare bulb austerity versus warm amber gel for intimacy
Helen's fur coat versus Jo's functional clothing — class and aspiration

flashcard_questions.q: What is a practical in stage lighting?
flashcard_questions.a: A visible stage lamp (table lamp, bare bulb) that motivates the scene's light quality.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a gel in lighting design?
flashcard_questions.a: A colour filter placed in front of a lantern to change the colour of the emitted light.
The general lighting condition covering the stage at any given point in a production.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a gobo do in lighting design?
flashcard_questions.a: A cut-out plate inserted into a profile lantern to project a pattern or texture onto the stage.
A focused beam designed to illuminate a single performer or small area, drawing audience focus.

flashcard_questions.q: What is set design in drama?
flashcard_questions.a: The constructed physical environment that locates action and carries symbolic meaning.

flashcard_questions.q: What is a prop as symbol?
flashcard_questions.a: A stage object that carries symbolic meaning beyond its practical function.

flashcard_questions.q: What is costume choice in drama?
flashcard_questions.a: The silhouette, fabric, colour and fit of a garment chosen to communicate character, period and status.
A pre-recorded or live sound effect used to signal location, time or emotional atmosphere.
A lantern producing a soft-edged beam, useful for warm domestic or naturalistic scenes.

flashcard_questions.q: What type of lantern produces a sharply defined beam for tight lighting specials?

flashcard_questions.a: Staging that accurately reproduces the physical details of the real world using realistic set and props.

glossary_terms.definition: The physical constructed environment within which the action of a play takes place, including furniture, levels, materials and symbolic objects.
A staging style that accurately reproduces the physical details of the real world, using realistic set pieces, props and costumes.
An object on stage that carries symbolic meaning beyond its practical function.
A visible stage lamp such as a table lamp or bare bulb that motivates the quality of the artificial light in a scene.
A colour filter placed in front of a lantern to change the colour of the light it emits.
The general lighting condition covering the stage at any given point in a production.
A focused beam of light designed to illuminate a single performer or small area, used to draw focus or isolate a moment.
A metal plate with a cut-out pattern inserted into a profile lantern to project a shape or texture onto the stage.
A pre-recorded or live sound effect used to signal location, time of day or emotional atmosphere in a production.
The silhouette, fabric, colour and fit of a garment as chosen by a costume designer to communicate character, period and status.
The way a performer uses their body, posture and movement to communicate character.
